title: Hutton Discovers Deep Time
objective: After this level you can explain how James Hutton read tilted rock layers to argue that Earth is immensely old.
summary: James Hutton argued in 1785 that slow, repeating cycles shaped Earth. At Siccar Point in 1788, tilted layers under red sandstone showed him how much time that took.

cards.headline: In 1788, a rocky Scottish point showed that Earth is unimaginably old.
cards.body: A widely held view in Hutton's day was that Earth was about 6,000 years old. One cliff on the Scottish coast gave James Hutton striking proof that it was far, far older. What did he see?

cards.headline: Hutton's big idea
cards.body: James Hutton, a Scottish geologist, watched ordinary things happen: rain and rivers wearing land down, sediment settling in the sea, layers hardening into rock, land being pushed up again. In 1785 he argued that these slow cycles had repeated many times over. If everyday processes built the whole landscape, the age of the Earth had to be inconceivably great. Small changes, repeated long enough, build a planet.

cards.headline: Two sets of rock at an angle
cards.body: In June 1788, Hutton visited Siccar Point with his friends John Playfair and James Hall. There, layers of greywacke sandstone and mudstone stand nearly vertical. Across their worn tops lie younger, gently sloping layers of red sandstone. Where two sets of rock formed at different times meet like this, geologists call it an unconformity.

cards.headline: Reading the gap
cards.body: Sediment settles in flat layers, so Hutton read the cliff as a story in steps. Flat layers formed under the sea. They were tilted on end and raised above the water. Erosion wore them down. They sank again and were buried under new flat layers. Every step is slow, and the whole sequence needs an enormous stretch of time. Playfair called it looking into "the abyss of time."
cards.callout: Laid flat, tilted up, worn down, buried again

cards.headline: Deep time: discovered
learned: Hutton: slow, repeating cycles need vast time
At Siccar Point, vertical layers sit under red sandstone
An unconformity is a gap between two sets of rock
Tilt, erode, bury: each step takes ages

questions.prompt: What did Hutton see at Siccar Point?

options.label: A volcano erupting through layers of sandstone
options.rationale: Siccar Point is a cliff of sedimentary layers, not a volcano.

options.label: Nearly vertical layers under gently sloping red sandstone
Flat layers stacked neatly from bottom to top
options.rationale: The lower layers stand nearly on end.

options.label: Fossil shells scattered on a sandy beach
options.rationale: The clue was the angle between two sets of rock.

questions.explanation: Nearly vertical greywacke is covered by younger, gently sloping red sandstone: an unconformity.

questions.prompt: Put Hutton's story of Siccar Point in order.
questions.explanation: The layers were laid flat under the sea, tilted up, worn down by erosion and then buried again under new flat layers.

questions.prompt: The red sandstone on top at Siccar Point started as loose sand. How did that sand become rock?

options.label: It was compacted and cemented by minerals
It melted underground and cooled
options.rationale: Melting and cooling makes igneous rock.

options.label: Sunlight baked it hard on the beach
options.rationale: Sand turns to rock after burial, not in the sun.

options.label: Heat and pressure lined up its minerals into sheets

questions.explanation: Buried sand is compacted by the layers above and cemented by minerals crystallizing between the grains.
